Hydrogen gas is a potential clean energy source. It is mainly produced from the electrolysis of water. In the presence of acid, water ionizes as 2H₂O → H++ OH⁻ These ions formed move towards the opposite electrodes.
At the cathode (negative electrode): 2H+ + 2e⁻ → H₂(g)
CHEMISTRY, GRADE 11 | 232
At the anode (positive electrode): 4OH- → O₂(g) + 2H2O + 4e⁻ The overall reaction for the electrolysis of water: 2H₂O → 2H₂ + O₂ The product of electrolysis depends upon
a. nature of electrolyte (whether it is molten or aqueous) b. nature of electrodes (whether it is active or inert)

Why is acid or salt added to pure water for the electrolysis of water? Pure water has only 10-7 M H+ ions and 10-7 M OH – ions. These very small quantities of ions are not enough to conduct the current. Acid or salt added produces sufficient number of ions to conduct electricity. A. Electrolysis of molten NaCl using Pt electrodes.

Fig: electrolysis of molten NaCl A Down’s cell is a commercial electrochemical cell used to obtain sodium metal. This process involves the electrolysis of molten sodium chloride using Pt (inert) electrodes. The reaction at anode and cathode are at cathode. Electrolysis of aqueous NaCl solution using Pt electrodes When aqueous solution (salt dissolved in water) is used as an electrolyte, both the salt and the water take part in the reaction and form different types of ions. If there are different kinds of ions

near an electrode, the ones that need the least energy (lowest discharge potential) will be changed into products.
Consider the electrolysis of aqueous solution of NaCl.
The potential at which the ion is discharged or deposited on the appropriate electrode is termed the discharge or deposition potential.
The decreasing order of discharge potential of some of the ions is given below,
Both NaCl and water ionizes,
For cations:

NaCl → Na++ Cl- H2O → H++OH- At the anode, both Cl- and OH- ions move but discharge potential of Clion is less than that of OH-. It means it is easier for Cl- to change into Cl2 than the OH- ion to O2.
Li+ >K+ >Na+> Ca++ >Mg++ >Al+++> Zn++> Fe++> Ni++> H+ >Cu++> Hg+> Au+++ For anions:
SO4- - >NO3-> OH- >Cl-> Br->I-
2Cl⁻ → Cl₂(g) + 2e⁻
At cathode, both H+ and Na+ ion move but the discharge potential of H+ is lower than that of Na+. So, it is easier for H+ to become H2 than Na+. 2H₂O + 2e⁻ → H₂(g) + 2OH-
So, the products of electrolysis of aqueous solution of NaCl is H2 and Cl2 respectively at cathode and anode.
C. Electrolysis of Copper sulphate solution using platinum and copper electrodes.
Fig: electrolysis of CuSO4 solution using (I)graphite (inert)electrodes and (II)Copper(active) electrodes
In both cases, the ionization of copper sulphate and water occur as follows:
CuSO4 → Cu2+ and SO42−
H2O →H+ and OH− ions
The reaction at cathode is same for both the cases.
CHEMISTRY, GRADE 11 | 234
Cu2++2e−→Cu [As Cu2+ has lower discharge potential than H+, it is reduced first]
Using platinum (inert) electrodes At anode, As OH− has lower discharge potential than SO42−, it gets preferentially oxidised.
OH- → O2(g) + H2O + 4eHence, Cu at cathode and O2 at anode are produced by electrolysis.
Using copper electrodes (active) At anode, Cu oxidizes prior to the oxidation of OH- and SO4- Cu →Cu+ + At the end, copper at anode becomes thin whereas copper at cathode becomes thick in size.
The reaction at anode is different due to different nature of the electrodes.
